Regarding the Non-Self of Phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*): if there were such a thing as a self-view, it would be subsumed under [false] views.

When a Bodhisattva enters the Samādhi of Correspondence (*anuloma-samādhi*), they no longer engage in such discrimination. This very observation constitutes the skillful means for entering [the path]. The Bodhisattva...
Thus, there is no discrimination regarding persons;
all phenomena are likewise without discrimination.
There are two types: aspiration and the gathering of the distracted.
This is the dwelling in all skillful means (*upāya*).
Not dwelling in the notion of phenomena (*dharmasaṃjñā*) demonstrates non-discrimination.
This, then, concludes the transmission by exhorting one to cultivate the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmaśūnyatā*) while not dwelling in that emptiness of phenomena.
The abbreviations are the same, yet knowledge, vision, and faith are not clear.
Why is that? Because it is said:
"It reveals the higher mind and higher wisdom."
Within non-conceptuality, there is knowledge, vision,
and resolute conviction. Here, "knowledge" relies upon śamatha,
while "vision" relies upon vipaśyanā.
These two types of resolute conviction (adhimokṣa) rely upon samādhi;
resolute conviction is precisely faith (śraddhā),
and śamatha is the higher training in mind (adhicitta).
Vipaśyanā is precisely *adhiprajñā* (supreme wisdom).
Samādhi is the mastery of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
According to this, these three are for those who proceed directly.
This is the practice of subduing through the Mahāyāna;
it is not for those of sudden enlightenment,
but for those who abide in the Supreme Vehicle.
That [attainment] is difficult to understand and difficult to enter over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*;
this is easily realized and easily attained in a single *kṣaṇa*,
as is fully detailed in the biographies.
I have explained this extensively within [the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*].
Vasubandhu considered "knowing" to be conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*),
while "seeing" is ultimate knowledge (*paramārtha-jñāna*).
To believe that this is samādhi is to miss the essential purport of the sūtra;
for it involves perceiving dharmas and perceiving a self, rather than perceiving True Suchness (tathatā).
According to this, even the perception of phenomena does not perceive *tathatā* (suchness),
let alone perceive a self.
Thus, worldly wisdom consists in knowing existence and knowing non-existence.
The wisdom of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-jñāna) is the vision of reality;
conventional samādhi is the abiding in faith through the departure from [the extremes of] existence and non-existence.
If there were neither existence nor non-existence, what would be called worldly wisdom (loka-jñāna)?
If there were neither the ultimate nor the conventional, how could there be the supreme truth?
If one does not abide in detachment, who can enter samādhi?
Originally, it is through concentration that wisdom is generated; this is the universal gateway of the Three Baskets.
If one follows this statement, then faith should indeed come first and seeing-and-knowing (*jñāna-darśana*) should follow;
one must not say "knowing-and-seeing-then-faith.
The distinction between these names is, for now, as in the preceding examples.
According to this scriptural passage,
it proclaims the essence of the fruit of eternally abiding wisdom— the ultimate state of the two bodies, the True and the Transformational.
The six metaphors and three meanings are clearly manifest in direct realization.
The ten stages of the sages and the three levels of the worthies cultivate themselves until they are clear and bright.
Therefore, the Tathāgata cites this as the correct entry to exhort them toward the True Vehicle; it is not intended to separately clarify meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
This, then, employs the three non-existences exclusively to eliminate self-nature.
Although it is said that there are two types of self, they ultimately constitute a single emptiness.
That being so, the imagined characteristic of the self is falsely existent and false, and thus need only be known;
the dependent view of the self is provisionally existent and provisional, and thus must be seen.
One gains faith through the realization that the true nature of the self is realized;
thus, one does not abide in the perception of signlessness,
for this is the entry into the dharmas as they appear, which collectively constitute the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*).

Since these marks lack intrinsic nature, it is said that they "are not"; yet because they are my habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), it is said that they "are named. This, then, is the non-abiding emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
It is fully explained as in the traditional commentaries.
If the Buddhas, when teaching the Dharma, did not speak of the emanation body (nirmāṇakāya),
then who would say that Śākyamuni Tathāgata is an emanation? According to the facts,
since the Buddha's body manifests through the response of merit and teaches the Dharma, [he must be the actual Buddha].
What concern is this for the Buddha-body?
This is precisely the eternally abiding fundamental Dharma;
it is the Dharma spontaneously realized through conditions.
That being so, the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) is like a shadow or a reflected image;
as a dominant condition (adhipatipratyaya), when has it ever attained enlightenment, and when has it ever spoken?
Even if such a phenomenon were to exist, it could not express anything.
Because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is ineffable,
this is an exhortation for those who uphold the sutra to expound it without giving rise to the thought of "I" as the speaker, nor giving rise to the conceptualization of the meaning expressed.
It is like one who is confused about south being north and insists that it is not north.
They will ultimately not awaken.
If one awakens through self-realization without depending on another, it is clearly explained.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata has expounded this, and the Bodhisattvas have proclaimed it to these assemblies.
How could one's own power possibly suffice?
How much less so when both the speaker and the listener are merely traversing and realizing that which is their own mind,
all of which is devoid of intrinsic nature?
Just as space has no inherent nature of world-dust particles,
it is said:
"When I sat at the site of enlightenment, wisdom was unattainable."
"An empty fist deceives small children," so it is used to deliver all beings;
this is precisely the initial mirror of Bodhi and the subsequent mind of non-nature.
Alternatively, it expounds the Dharma-gates of conventional truth.
Some speak of the contemplation of the principle of *tathatā*, asserting that all objects of cognition lack intrinsic nature and are merely one's own mind; thus, there would be no defilement.
This, however, cannot be called a true teaching.
To speak in this manner is called speaking the truth. Therefore,
compared to upholding even a single four-line verse,
the Bodhisattva’s perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) is not its equal.
It is precisely for this reason that Asaṅga stated:
"One is unstained by birth and death."
Maitreya says:
"Not abiding in nirvana.
This [statement] and the preceding one correspond to one another from both internal and external perspectives, serving together to eliminate doubt.
According to this verse, the four lines consist of three layers:
first, pointing to the Dharma; second, citing an analogy; and third, exhorting practice.
Maitreya said:
It is neither conditioned nor is it apart from the nirvāṇa of all Tathāgatas;
this is the dispelling of doubt.
Why? If the Dharma were taught eternally, who would enter nirvāṇa?
Therefore it is said:
"The Buddha attains nirvana and manifests transformation bodies (nirmāṇakāya) to preach the Dharma.
This preaching of the Dharma by the transformation body is not unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
The Buddha’s attainment of nirvāṇa is not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, neither abiding in existence nor non-existence is the dharma-gate of exhaustion (*kṣaya-dharmamukha*);
it is merely a distinct practice of the bodhisattva.
One must not interpret the Tathāgata in such a way.
If that were so, the Reward Buddha (vipākabuddha) would have a beginning but no end.
If his entry into nirvāṇa were no different from that of a transformation body (nirmāṇakāya), then the Tathāgata neither comes nor speaks.
This is exactly as explained above.
How could one claim, based on the mental scope of a bodhisattva, that a Buddha does not abide in either the conditioned or the unconditioned?
As for the fruit of srotāpanna, it already transcends the categories of existence and non-existence.
How much more so the Buddha’s wisdom!
As the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra says:
"I contemplate the Tathāgata."
It does not come from the past, it does not abide in the present, and it does not go to the future.
It does not even belong to this shore, nor to the other shore, nor to the middle stream.
It is neither conditioned nor unconditioned.
That which cannot be cognized by consciousness and cannot be known by wisdom is called right contemplation;
this is called seeing the Buddha.
Thus, we know that [the teaching] was expounded in accordance with the capacities of those to be trained.
Thus it is said that one does not abide in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa,
because the nature of those two cannot be apprehended. Furthermore,
regarding the statement that contemplating the Buddha means to be free from both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Since those two are considered to be the mind and its measurements,
and since there is neither coming nor going before or after,
who is it that speaks in the interim?
To instead use a world of minute atoms to explain pure empty space—
is this not the height of delusion?
If one follows that interpretation, [it would be so].
One should then say: "The nirvāṇa of a single bodhisattva is neither conditioned nor non-conditioned.
Why? Because "exhaustion" and "non-exhaustion" are terms that apply to all bodhisattvas, not to individual bodhisattvas. This is what the Bodhisattva Gandhavyūha meant.
According to the *Nirvāṇa*, this is translated as "quiescent rest.
How could there be existence or non-existence without such quiescent rest?
Thus, within the wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmyajñāna*), one has already departed from the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) intrinsic nature of *tathatā*.
How much more so for the most pure awakening?
Furthermore, apart from the wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmyajñāna*), how could one abide without dwelling in existence or non-existence?
As explained above.
In the "Fruition and Severance" chapter, Maitreya is correctly explained through nine matters used as metaphors for nine dharmas,
which are combined into three groups.
One essence, two functions, and three activities: consciousness, objects, and faculties constitute the essence;
the physical body and its sensations constitute the function;
and the past, present, and future constitute the activity.
The treatise states:
Regarding "the consciousness of the perceived and the perceiver," "perceiving" refers to the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), which is the consciousness capable of apprehension.
The "characteristic" (nimitta) is the consciousness that is the object of the image-aspect (nimittabhāga);
the "consciousness" (vijñāna) is the consciousness of the body, the self, and the experiencer.
These are not mutually contradictory.
Thus, consciousness is the act of discerning.
Stars possess radiance;
yet when the full moon is clear and bright, the small stars fade into obscurity.
Just as when the sun shines, the great stars do not appear,
so too when the wisdom arising from hearing and reflection gives rise to conceptualization, subtle right wisdom arises and that consciousness is extinguished;
this is the correspondence for their mutual exclusion.

Furthermore, when the characteristics of the six sense objects appear and the perceptions of the six consciousnesses arise, the empty flowers manifest within one's gaze because the visual impairment can give rise to these appearances; this is due to the commonality of the seeing.

The perfection of the six faculties is achieved through the combination of earth, water, fire, and wind, where the lamp, the scene, and the illumination depend on the oil, the vessel, the wick, and the flame together to produce light; this is due to the commonality of these conditions.
The vessel is the dependent retribution (niśraya-vipāka), arising from the enjoyment of others; illusion is a false object, arising from medicinal herbs dependent on others.
These are alike in that they do not arise of themselves.
The body is the primary retribution (mukhya-vipāka), formed from karmic seeds; dew is an accumulation of vapor caused by the coolness of night.
There is this commonality regarding the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
"Feeling" refers to the three types of feeling;
they are experienced by relying upon the primary and secondary elements.
Bubbles are stirred by water;
they are produced from wind and rain.
This is similar to [their] existence through contact.
Past karmic conditions are like the delusive objects of a dream that one recognizes as false upon waking;
this is the same as the present condition.
The present is provisionally existent, with moments of thought ceasinglessly succeeding one another.
A flash of lightning appears and vanishes in every new moment;
this rapidity is identical [to the process of rebirth].
Regarding the relationship between seeds and their retributions, the retribution occurs in the future life.
Just as when clouds gather but rain has not yet fallen,
there is a similarity in what follows later.
It is by means of these nine contemplations that [this is established].
The Buddha has attained mastery over conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma).
Thus, the verse says:
"Observing characteristics and enjoyments, and observing the events of the three times."
"Among conditioned phenomena, one attains stainless mastery"—
according to this, one attains mastery over the conditioned,
but not so regarding the unconditioned.
Why is this? Because these nine kinds [of wisdom] contemplate only the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
As the preceding verse states:
"Because of the correct contemplation of sublime wisdom."
I do not yet understand whether this wisdom belongs to the Bodhisattva or is entrusted to the Tathāgata.
If it belongs to the Bodhisattva, one cannot say that all Tathāgatas have entered nirvāṇa;
if it is the Tathāgata, one cannot say that one should contemplate in such a manner.
If the relationship between teacher and disciple is still not clearly understood,
how can the meaning of the text be comprehended? If these nine similes do not clarify the three natures,
they must instead be explained as distinct illustrations of the nine types of contemplation.
I do not yet know how to practice the contemplation on [the body] as being like stars.
When stars appear as points of light amidst darkness,
does one give rise to the perception of darkness, or does one give rise to a mind of clarity?
If one gives rise to the illumination of wisdom, this constitutes the contemplation that eliminates stars;
one must not say it is "like a star.
It is also like the contemplation of a visual impairment (*timira*).
Thus, the object arises from the cataract;
if the cognition arises without removing it, the cataract-object will constantly manifest.
If the cataract-object is removed, that is precisely the contemplation that removes the cataract.
It cannot be said that it is like a visual impairment.
It is also like observing with a lamp;
the lamp arises from a multitude of conditions.
The sense faculties arise from the four great elements.
If one knows that they arise from conditions, what can be attained?
If, because they arise from conditions, the lamp has no intrinsic nature, [then so it is with the faculties].
This is precisely the refutation of the "lamp-observation" analogy;
one cannot claim that it is like a lamp.
All six subsequent metaphors are likewise refuted in this same manner.
Thus, one should know that the exhortation to cultivate the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā) and the metaphors used to reveal the absence of intrinsic nature constitute the true treatise.
Furthermore, these nine types are all comprised within the eighteen elements (aṣṭādaśa-dhātu), which consist of objects of enjoyment and karmic activities.
There are no eight minds or mental factors;
even if one were to contemplate the ninefold accomplishment,
it would merely be the emptiness of persons, as it excludes only conditioned phenomena.
Because it does not exhaustively encompass all phenomena;
for among all phenomena there are six unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) things.
This "all" refers to...
Because all one hundred dharmas collectively constitute the two kinds of selflessness,
Asaṅga states:
"This reveals the four characteristics of the conditioned."
1. The characteristic of intrinsic nature;
2. The characteristic of attachment to the flavor of what is dwelt upon;
3. The characteristic of conforming to faults.
Fourth is the characteristic of conformity to renunciation.
Although these four groups of nine are each distinct,
they do not differ in their status as conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
That being so, it is appropriate to regard the person and phenomena as like a visual impairment (*timira*).
To fail to understand these various metaphors is incorrect.
Furthermore, by conforming to the selflessness of persons and phenomena, one attains liberation because of the absence of cognitive grasping (*ālambana*).
Thus, knowing that the activities of the three periods of time have already arisen, one penetrates non-self;
this demonstrates the characteristic of conforming to renunciation.
The remaining explanations are largely the same as those of Vasubandhu.
According to this [explanation] regarding renunciation, there would be neither persons nor dharmas;
to collectively designate them as "conditioned" (saṃskṛta) would contradict the "hundred dharmas" and the doctrine of selflessness. Why?

For instance, the characteristic of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-lakṣaṇa) is a common characteristic (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa); even the seeing-consciousness and suchness are manifested by the common characteristics of all dharmas.
Is it not that they possess their own intrinsic nature?
If they lacked an intrinsic nature,
one could not speak of six kinds of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
Since they are differentiated and distinct,
it is clear that each possesses its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Thus, within the characteristics of these intrinsic natures, how could the nature of the "existence" and "non-existence" propositions be present?
The word "only" refers to the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, the characteristic of transcendence (*niḥsaraṇa*) is the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*); this is transcendence.
It is neither outside of the conditioned and the unconditioned, nor in between them.
Since even the unconditioned is itself transcendent,
how could it enter the four types of the conditioned?
How can names and meanings be so discordant and erroneous?
Therefore, we know that the four marks to which one clings are all devoid of intrinsic nature.
This is fully contained in the biographical accounts.
Thus, the *Dunben* (Fundamental Cessation) states:
"Whatever is performed through the conjunction of conditions is either conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)."
Many Mahāyāna sūtras frequently employ this analogy;
they may present it as one, two, seven, nine, or ten,
or as extensively as in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*.
All metaphors are used to illustrate the sublime virtues of the body and to illustrate sentient beings;
Dharmodgata is used as a metaphor for the Tathāgata—how could a mere star or a shadow serve as a definitive metaphor for their meeting?

Therefore, one should know that by using easily understood emptiness to illustrate emptiness that is difficult to understand, it follows that within emptiness, even the realms of dust and the two bodies—the true body and the response body—lack intrinsic nature; how much more so, then, for all other phenomena?
Therefore, these nine metaphors are employed to universally clarify that the three absences are all devoid of an intrinsic nature;
this constitutes the correct explanation.
Question:
We have already heard about the mind and mental factors.
Regarding the objects of the five eyes, we have heard of six kinds of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
Within the discourse on the four fruits, eleven types of matter are explained.
Within the diagram of the eight consciousnesses, please set forth the twenty-four dissociated [factors]. Answer:
There are, in brief, twenty-four kinds of dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
First, acquisition;
second, the life-faculty;
third, the homogeneous character of the group.
4. The state of being an ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva).
5. The attainment of non-conception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti).
6. The attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
7. The matter of non-perception;
8. the name-body (nāmakāya);
9. the phrase-body (padakāya).
10. The aggregate of words (nāmakāya); 11.
Birth; 12. Old age.
Thirteen: abiding;
fourteen: impermanence;
fifteen: transmigration.
16. Distinctness; 17. Association;
18. Rapid succession.
Nineteenth, the sequence;
twentieth, the directions;
twenty-first, the time.
Twenty-two: number.
Twenty-three: the nature of combination.
Twenty-four: the nature of non-combination.
Question:
If, when preaching the Dharma, one commits the fault of contradicting the various sūtras or engages in malicious scholastic debate, one falls into the four evil destinies.
Since the Buddha has given explicit statements on this, how can you disparage the various sūtras and śāstras?
Furthermore, regarding those who claim that the interpretations of Asaṅga and Vasubandhu slander the Sages and will cause them to fall into a great abyss—
how can they understand this for themselves?
Answer:
According to the Lotus Sūtra, it says:
"The faculties of sentient beings are dull; they are attached to pleasure and blinded by ignorance. How can such as these be delivered?"
"I would rather not preach the Dharma and quickly enter nirvana.
Then, reflecting upon the power of skillful means employed by the Buddhas of the past, [he thought:
"The path I have now attained should likewise be taught as the three vehicles."
Now, for those sentient beings whose virtuous seeds have matured and who possess wisdom and sharp faculties,
the Buddha does not speak of the three vehicles but proclaims only the single reality.
This is what is called "the mark of the quiescence of all dharmas."
It cannot be proclaimed in words;
this is the principle of the single reality, wherein the characteristics of the known and the knower are quiescent by nature.
It is where the path of language is cut off.
Therefore, one should know that it is not only for those three types of beings; humans and devas must also be guided and led.
For this reason, the five precepts, the ten wholesome actions, the four dhyānas, and the four formless attainments are taught.
Yet, there are those who harbor a sense of weariness toward worldly life.
Although the resolve to enter the Truth has not yet been deeply cultivated,
one must therefore universally teach non-arising to eliminate the [notions of] person and self;
this constitutes the distinction between Nirvana, the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
Just as a mani jewel, though devoid of intention, fulfills each request, so it is that if a sick person begs for medicine, they may obtain it;
however, they can never attain what lies beyond their expectations.
The Buddha’s teaching is likewise.
All others have been omitted here.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
If that mind is extinguished, there is neither vehicle nor rider, and no establishment of a vehicle;
therefore, I speak of it as the One Vehicle.
Thus, one should know that without those five types of spiritual faculties, the One Vehicle would not be established.
Since it has been taught that there are differences in depth and shallowness,
it follows that the latter one is exclusively the Buddha Vehicle,
while the former four are not the Buddha's teachings at all.
Alternatively, one may doubt the celestial vehicle (*devayāna*) by means of human dharmas;
or doubt the latter one by means of the former four;
or doubt the former four by means of the latter one.
Even extending to the five aspects of doubt for each of the five [vehicles], twenty-five layers of obstruction would result.
Yet, since these are applied according to the capacities of beings without impediment, how could there be any contradiction?
Furthermore, within each single vehicle itself, there are inherent levels of depth and shallowness.
In this regard, the webs of delusion and doubt increase;
is it not because while the spoken words are sufficient for profound understanding, one's own cognitive illumination is naturally shallow?
For instance, even in the minor contemplation of impurity, there exist both correct and erroneous perceptions.
If one perceives the appearance of the Buddha only when it is impure,
then such contemplation is contrary to reality and constitutes a false observation.
How much more so, then, could one who observes the Buddha and perceives an impure appearance be said to possess right observation?
For those of the Small Vehicle disposition,
if one were to preach the Mahāyāna to them, they would slander it, refuse to accept it, and fall into a great abyss.
This is precisely why, during the twenty-one days, he contemplated and did not preach the One Vehicle.
How much more so when one is correctly expounding the Buddha Vehicle,
yet intermingles it with the teachings for śrāvakas, humans, and devas presented in isolation;
is this not indeed delusion?
However, there are those who provide explanations by using the teachings of sound to explain the Buddha-dharma,
or by using the Buddha-dharma to explain the teachings of humans and devas.
Or, one might explain the dharmas of the ten stages by means of the dharmas of the first stage;
although this may be the correct teaching for that original vehicle,
when applied to elucidate this path, it is precisely a false statement.
How much more so regarding awakening and entry!
The True Dharma is pure, wondrously enlightened, without nature and without attainment, standing beyond the five vehicles.
To intermingle it with the signless and the non-arising is already extremely unacceptable.

How much more so when one attempts to establish the realization of the truths (abhisamaya) by means of worldly concepts such as suffering, emptiness, impermanence, non-self, the conditioned, and the unconditioned?
Alas, alas! How extreme is this delusion and error!
How do we know this is so?
According to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, it says:
"Those who have not yet attained true wisdom..."
The Awakened One (the Buddha) can be inferred within the context of *vijñapti-mātra* through scripture (*āgama*) and reasoning (*yukti*).
As Vasubandhu’s commentary states:
"Although not yet directly realized, [the Buddha] is known by means of authoritative scripture and by means of inference."
The true knowledge of consciousness-only (vijñaptimātra) should be known through inference;
therefore, it is known that the authoritative teaching refers to the sūtras of definitive meaning (nītārtha),
whereas that which is not the authoritative teaching refers to those of non-definitive meaning (neyārtha).
Furthermore, take for instance measurements and weights:
throughout the world, the regulations and statutes are uniform, and across the four seas they do not differ.
Yet, if one uses narrow widths or large spans that exceed established standards, such errors result in transgressions that deviate from the constant norms.
Thus, one does not personally follow them nor does one personally compare them.
Having already accepted those matters, one further implicates the virtuous by acting with deliberate intent;

how could this be called upholding public integrity? As for the four measures and the four reliances, they serve as a standard for those who have not yet attained realization, universally validating all principles and providing a framework for all sutras and treatises.
How could one not follow it?
How could one willfully contravene it?
How can one, having already received and upheld it, refrain from weighing its meaning while yet holding others accountable for their adherence?
How could one then hold them accountable for such comparisons?
Thus we know that the direct teachings given according to the capacities of beings are fundamentally not in conflict;
it is only those who measure falsely and the deluded and ignorant whose explanations are erroneous and discordant.
This would result in the fault of contradiction with the various sūtras;
for Māra would find an opportunity and one would fall into the three miserable realms oneself.
Therefore, it is said that those who discuss the meaning with a virtuous mind are reborn in the five Pure Abodes.
Those who propound doctrines with an evil mind fall into the four miserable realms;
this transmission clarifies that realization and entry alone constitute true awakening.
Should one deviate from this contemplation, one has nothing upon which to rely.
Furthermore, even the wisdom that awakens to the true exposition is merely a figurative designation;
how much more so the measure of what is manifested by one's own mind as the ultimate reality?
This is why there are similarities and differences.
It is precisely for this reason.
Thus we know that once pure awakening is proclaimed, merit and wisdom become inexhaustible.
Because they are able to repudiate all that is deviant and delusory,
those who follow such [views] from the outset will incur immeasurable karmic offenses.
Since they destroy and extinguish perfect illumination, it is not only their own persons that remain stagnant in the Willow Forest (the realm of hungry ghosts).
It is also the reason why sentient beings are deluded and misled.
As Asaṅga said:
"Ordinary people are unable to awaken to, know, or have faith in this profound and great Dharma."
The people of the world are for the most part like this; for this reason, this Dharma has fallen into ruin and desuetude.
Originally, the descent of the Buddhas into the world occurs at vast intervals and is difficult to encounter;
even if one should encounter them, it is even more difficult to hear the Dharma.
To hear the Dharma is difficult; to hear the profound Dharma is even more difficult;
and to have faith, understanding, and realization upon hearing the profound Dharma is most difficult of all.
Thus, realization or non-realization depends on whether one is diligent or not; it does not depend on hearing the teachings.
I pray that those who dwell together in this practice will not disparage themselves nor abandon themselves, as the verse says: [Insert Verse Here]
One accumulates all manner of desires without ever finding satisfaction; yet while still unsated by desire, one’s life comes to an end.
At the moment of death, neither wife, children, precious treasures, nor fame and status will follow;
only generosity, ethical discipline, and heedfulness shall be one’s companions in this future life.
The Commentary on the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Outer Commentary, Volume II.
